Tirukkuraḷ
(‘holy [treatise composed in the] metre “kuraḷ-veṇbā” ’)
------------------------------------------
The Tirukkuraḷ is an ancient didactical work in Tamil, which is extremely popular even today. It perhaps got this name since it is composed in the special metre called ‘kuraḷ-veṇbā’. The prefix ‘tiru’ is the Tamil substitute for the Sanskrit ‘Śrī’, showing respect.
Muppāl (group of three) is the other name by which it is known since it deals with the three पुरुषार्थस्. (See PURUṢĀRTHAS.)
Its famous author is तिरुवऌऌउवर् who might have lived in the 1st century A. D. Actually, Vaḷḷuvar is the name of one of the lowest castes of the pariah group. In the olden days they were employed by the kings and rulers to make royal announcements by beating drums (tom-tom). The author belonged to that caste and his actual name has been buried in the womb of history.
TiruvaḷḷuvarTiruvaḷḷuvar is said to have lived in Mylapore (now a part of the city of Madras or Chennai). He was a weaver by profession. According to the local legends he was an orphan abandoned by his real parents, but brought up by a couple of the vellāḷa (farmer) caste. His contact with holy men at a tender age of five made him inclined towards a spiritual life, which ultimately resulted in his becoming a saintly person. His wife वासुकि proved to be an ideal companion for him. She died earlier than him. Later, he embraced monastic life and engaged himself in spreading spiritual knowledge and wisdom. His work, the Tirukkuraḷ, when presented before the Saṅgam (assembly of great scholars) at मदुरै (in Tamil Nadu), was thoroughly examined and then acclaimed as a great work.
The work has 133 chapters, each containing 10 verses, the total thus being 1330 verses. They have been divided into three sections dealing with the first three pururṣārthas, as follows:
Arattuppāl(Section on Dharma—38 Chapters); Porutpāl(Section on Artha—70 Chapters); Kāmattupāl(Section on Kāma—25 Chapters). A brief synopsis of the subjects treated may now be given:
Arattuppāl
In praise of God; on rain; greatness of renunciation; on धर्म; family life; होस्पितलित्य् and kindness as also sweet words; gratitude; right conduct; evils to be avoided like envy and backbiting; on liberality; not eating meat; on penance; on truth; on true knowledge as also fate.
Porutpāl
Who a real king is; true marks of a good king; various actions and policies to be followed by a king; righteous rule versus tyranny; on spies; on embassies; on fortresses and acquisition of wealth; on the importance of the army; on friendship with others kings and allies; things to be avoided like इग्नोरन्चे and discord; wine and women; need to cultivate good conduct and modesty.
Kāmattupāl
This section deals with, in detail, various aspects of काम (erotic love) in a couple, before मर्रिअगे, in the married life, during pangs of separation and so on. Unlike some Sanskrit works on erotics, this section is much more decent and refined.
Though the Tirukkuraḷ deals with only the first three पुरुषार्थस्, the fourth puruṣārtha (mokṣa or लिबेरतिओन्) has been indirectly dealt with in chapters 1, 3, and 4.
There are ten commentaries (all in Tamil) on this work. Out of them, the one by Parimel Azhakar is considered the best.
Recently (in A.
) a huge statue of तिरुवऌऌउवर्, 40 metres or 133 feet in height, has been installed on the smaller rock in the sea near कन्याकुमारी (in Tamil Nadu).

Tirucendūr
------------------------------------------
Tirucendūr is one of the six pilgrim centres with a beautiful temple of Lord Muruga or सुब्रह्मण्य. It is situated at a distance of 55 kms. (34 miles) from Tirunelveli, the district headquarters in Tamil Nadu.
Though all the temples of सुब्रह्मण्य are generally built on the top of hillocks, this one is an exception built on seashore.
As per the local legends, Subrah-maṇya the commander-in-chief of the gods, made this place his base camp to fight the dreaded demon Surapadman. After a fight which lasted for six days, he killed the demon on the sixth day. The victory was celebrated on the seventh day.
While camping here, since Subrah-maṇya was eager to worship his ड़थेर् शिव, मय the celestial architect, built this temple for him. This is the origin of this temple.
Considered as a very ancient temple it must have undergone several additions and alterations, over the last thousand years.
The temple is situated so close to the sea that waves from the Gulf of Mannar constantly strike the eastern wall of the temple.
The front adjunct to the temple known as Ṣaṇmugavilāsam has 124 columns spread over an area of 36 metres (120 feet) by 26 metres (86 feet).
The Rājagopuram (main tower) is on the west instead of the east. It is 42 metres (137 feet) high and 27 metres (90 feet) wide.
The bathing ghat is said to contain nine tīrthas (holy waters) which can purify the devotees who take bath in it.
A little away from the temple, on the seashore there is a small well inside another which has crystal clear water. It is reputed to have been specially created by Lord Muruga to appease the thirst of his soldiers.
The major festivals celebrated at the temple campus are:
Vaikāsi Visagam in May-June
Āvani festival in August-September
Skanda festival for seven days in October-November
and Māsi festival for 12 days in February-March.

There are ten sub-temples in the nearby areas, the Veṅkaṭācalapati temple at Arumigu being the more popular one.
The temple administration is running an orphanage with 125 children.
Out of the few inscriptions in the campus, the one of 9th century A. D. is the earliest.

Tīrthayātrā
(‘going to holy places,’ ‘pilgrimage’)
------------------------------------------
Introduction
Tīrthayātrā or going to holy places or पिल्ग्रिमगे plays an extremely important part in a Hindu’s life.
Whereas the places of पिल्ग्रिमगे of other religions are mostly connected with the lives of their founders, those of हिन्दुइस्म् have the primary aim of elevating the minds of pilgrims to higher spiritual levels.
These pilgrim centres are legion and are spread all over India, from Amarnāth in the north to रामेश्वरम् in the south and Somnāth in the west up to पुरी in the east. If the sthalapurāṇas or the local legends have to be believed, these places are all extremely ancient, closely connected with the persons and incidents narrated in the epics and the पुराणस्. Of course, places associated with great saints and religious leaders of the historical period are also taken into consideration.
More often than not, these places of पिल्ग्रिमगे are situated in spots of natural scenery and beauty like mountain-tops, valleys, banks of rivers, islands, forests, seashore and other similar regions which are congenial to contemplation.
Over the centuries, वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् gradually faded out due to their inherent difficulties in performing them. Their place was soon taken up by pūjās (ritualistic worship), homas (oblations into consecrated fires associated with popular deities), vratas (religious vows) and tīrtha-yātras (pilgrimages). These were eulogised as easy to perform, but, giving equally good and quick results.
Literature
Literature on tīrthayātras is very extensive. In the Mahābhārata and the पुराणस् there are 40,000 verses concerning this subject.
They have been dealt with in independent treatises also.
Some of them are:
Kṛtya-kalpataruof Lakṣmīdhara(12th Century A. D.) Caturvargacintāmaṇi of Hemādri(13th Century A. D.) Tīrthacintāmaṇi of Vācaspati(15th Century A. D.) Tīrthasāra of Dalapati(circa A.

) Apart from these, there are separate treatises on individual places like गया and पुरी also.
Purpose of Tīrthayātrā
Tīrthayātrā has been listed as one of the sāmānyadharmas (universal or common duties) by some of the scriptures like the Viṣṇudharmasūktas (2.16, 17). It is supposed to destroy one’s sins, give religious merit and result in purity of मिन्द्. Even the Ṛgveda (10.75 खिल) refers to the holiness of the place where the white and the black rivers (Gaṅgā and यमुना) merge. A bath here enables one to go to हेअवेन्. One who drowns himself here attains अमृतत्व or इम्मोर्तलित्य्. The पुराणस् abound in such ideas.
The beauty and grandeur of such places conducive to a mood of meditation, as also association of spiritual giants who might have visited these places earlier and a host of related ideas have endowed these places of पिल्ग्रिमगे with spiritual vibrations. The etymological meaning of the word ‘īrtha’—tīryate anena iti tīrthaṁ, saṁsārasāgarataraṇopāya-bhūtaṁ; ‘that by which it is crossed, that which helps in crossing the ocean of transmigratory existence, is tīrtha’—also points towards this conclusion.
That is why when people visit these places with the right attitude, they are immensely benefited.
Classification of Tīrthas
The Brahmapurāṇa (70.16-19) classifies the tīrthas or places of पिल्ग्रिमगे into four groups:
daiva those that are created by gods.
āsura those associated with असुरस् or demons, like Gaya.
ārṣa Those established by ṛṣis or sages, like प्रभास and नर-नारायण.
mānuṣa those created by human beings, kings like अम्बरीष, मनु and कुरु.
These four are assigned to the four yugas—Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara and Kali—respectively (ibid 175.31-32).
However, this classification does not have much relevance to us today.
Eligibility for Tīrthayātrā
One of the questions that has often been discussed in the पुराणस् and the धर्मशास्त्रस् is that of अधिकार or eligibility for तीर्थयात्रा. This had probably become necessary because study of the वेदस् and performance of the Vedic rituals had been restricted only to the dvijas (the ‘twice-born’ classes, viz., the members of the first three castes).
Unlike the study of the वेदस् or performance of the Vedic rituals, taking recourse to तीर्थयात्रा is open to all human beings irrespective of their caste, status or condition (vide Matsyapurāṇa 184.66, 67). The पुराणस् go to the extent of declaring that those who take a bath in a holy river or at a holy place will not only attain लिबेरतिओन् themselves but also purify seven generations of their fore-fathers and descendants (Vāmanapurāṇa 36.78, 79).
Such hyperbolic eulogy was obviously meant to induce even the common folk to undertake तीर्थयात्रा.
Notwithstanding such liberal statements, some primary rules had also been imposed on those intending to perform it.
For instance:
A ब्रह्मचारिन् living in the गुरु’s होउसे had to take his permission.
Married persons were obliged to take their spouses also, failing which they would not get the religious merit of the पिल्ग्रिमगे!
Ethical Life, a Precondition
Despite eulogising तीर्थयात्रा in order to attract the common people, the sages of the पुराणस् did not fail to stress the importance of a moral and ethical life as a precondition, without which it would become futile. However, it was also conceded that persons—even transgressors of धर्म, and sinners—who undertake तीर्थयात्रा with faith, repent for their misdeeds and resolve not to repeat them, will definitely be benefited by it (vide Vāyupurāṇa 77.125).
Though persons leading a pure life do not need to undertake pilgrimages, they too will immensely be benefited in their spiritual evolution if they do.
It is interesting to note that the practice of virtues like ज्ञान (scriptural knowledge), kṣamā (forgiveness), दया (compassion) and दम (self-control) are themselves ‘tīrtha,’ since they are conducive to purity of मिन्द्. So also the company of holy persons (devotees of God वासुदेव).
Recommended Procedure
The पुराणस् and the धर्मशास्त्रस् have laid down the procedure to be followed in तीर्थयात्रा. The same may be briefly summarised as follows:
Fasting on the previous day; worship of the family deity, गणपति, and नवग्रहस् and giving gifts to the poor and the needy on the day of departure; wearing ochre-colored or yellow clothes; सङ्कल्प or religious resolve as dictated by the scriptures; giving up all articles of luxury and leading a simple, austere, life during the पिल्ग्रिमगे; after returning, repetition of the worship of the deities and offering gifts as a mark of thanksgiving.
In the modern context when even पिल्ग्रिमगे has become a part of tourism industry, one may just offer worship to the family deity, visit a temple of the same (or of one’s choice) and take the blessings of the elders before starting. The same may be repeated after the successful completion of the पिल्ग्रिमगे.
Pratinidhi System
In the olden days, it was a lifetime’s ambition for every devoted Hindu to visit काशी (and other holy places) at least once. However, during the times when transport and communication were extremely difficult, even able-bodied persons could not easily make it. Then what to speak of others handicapped by ill-health, lack of money, old-age disabilities and so on!
For the benefit of such persons, the treatises on तीर्थयात्रा have given a unique method called ‘pratinidhi-kriyā’. According to this, the person who is unable to perform the पिल्ग्रिमगे should request someone who is going, to perform some rite like bathing in the river गङ्गा, on his behalf also. After reaching the गङ्गा river, the pilgrim prepares an image of straw (kuśa-grass) and immerses it in the water with appropriate mantras. The person for whom this proxy rite is performed is said to get a part of the religious merit which he would have got if he had personally done it himself. (vide Atrismṛti 50 and 51).
Epilogue
Tīrthayātrā or पिल्ग्रिमगे to holy places has been an integral part of a Hindu’s religious life. If people, both in the ancient and in the medieval periods, were prepared to face all hardships and undertake pilgrimages, it was their deep faith in the system that sustained them. It also helped them to attain emotional integration with other Hindus throughout the country.
Today, with the tremendous advancement of science and technology in the fields of transportation and communication, it is possible to reach even the farthest point on the globe in a matter of hours! This has made pilgrimages not only easy and comfortable but also enjoyable. Only, the pilgrims should avoid the temptation of making the pilgrimages pleasure-trips, by trying sincerely to cultivate the same religious fervour our forefathers had.

tiryakpuṇḍra
(‘a religious mark placed crosswise [on the body]’)
------------------------------------------
Wearing a पुण्ड्र or a religious mark, especially on the forehead, is a must for every Hindu. The पुण्ड्र can be ūrdhva (upright or vertical) or tiryak (crosswise or horizontal). The latter is called तिर्यक्पुण्ड्र and is worn with भस्म (holy ash). (See BHASMA.)
This mark consists of three lines drawn crosswise, with भस्म, using three fingers of the right hand. These three lines are supposed to represent the three वेदस् (Ṛg, Yajus and Sāma), the three syllables a, u and m of the प्रणव, the three guṇas (sattva, रजस् and तमस्), the three śaktis of the Divine मोथेर् (jñānaśakti, इच्छाशक्ति, and क्रियाशक्ति) and so on. The whole idea seems to be to bring into one’s मिन्द्, the various religio-spiritual concepts so as to feel pure and elevated.

Tiruppāḍ
(‘holy songs’)
------------------------------------------
Kāraikkāl Ammaiyār (5th century A. D.) was one of the sixty three Nāyanmārs (Śaiva saints). She was known earlier as Punītavatī, the only offspring of a merchant, Dhanadattan. She had been married to Paramadattan, a rich merchant. She was a great devotee of Lord शिव endowed with mystical powers.
Later on, she became a wandering minstrel, singing devotional songs on शिव. These songs collected together are now known as Tiruppāḍ.

Tiruvāymoḷi
(‘divine words of a holy sage’)
------------------------------------------
This famous work in chaste classical Tamil language of नम्माऌवार् (See ĀḶVĀRS.) is the best and the longest among the Divyaprabandhams. It has 1102 pāśuras (verses), divided into ten sections (centums). Each of these again, has ten daśakas (decades) plus an additional concluding verse.
It is interesting to note that the pāśuras are in the ‘anta-ādi’ style. That is, the last word (anta) of one verse becomes the first (ādi) of the next.
The subject matter may briefly be summarised as follows:
Greatness of God; his several blessed qualities like compassion and protecting his devotees; relationship between the jīvātman (individual सोउल्) and परमात्मन् (God); भक्ति (devotion) and प्रपत्ति (self-surrender) as the primary means of attaining मोक्ष (liberation); the necessity of performing the allotted duties in life for self-purification.
In these prayers to the Lord, मधुरभाव (bridal म्य्स्तिचिस्म्) can be seen as an important aspect.
The pāśuras of this work have been set to मुसिच्.
There are several commentaries on this work. The very first one was by Tirukkurkai Pirān Piḷḷān in 6000 verses. But the most voluminous—and also the most famous—one is the Īḍu of Vaḍakku Tiruvīdhi Piḷḷai.
See also प्रबन्धम्">DIVYAPRABANDHAM.

Tirunallar
------------------------------------------
One of the nine planetary deities, शनि or Śanaiścara, is more feared than loved since he is the lord of afflictions. Though separate temples dedicated to him are not very common, we have one at तिरुनल्लर्, just 5 kms. (3 miles) to the west of the town Karaikal in the Puduchery (or Pondicherry) State.
It is actually a minor temple in the complex of the bigger शिव temple called Darbhāraṇyeśvara Temple situated on the south bank of कावेरी.
According to the local legends the शिवलिङ्ग was discovered in a forest covered with the दर्भ grass (Poa-cyno- suriodes) by ब्रह्मा the creator himself. Feeling happy about it he mentally worshipped it and built a temple round it decorating it with navaratnas (nine gems). The temple has therefore came to be known as Darbhāraṇyeśvara Temple.
Using his दण्ड (holy stick) he dug a tank, known as Brahmadaṇḍa-tīrtham. Thereafter इन्द्र and other deities also created such holy tanks.
Darbhāraṇyeśvara is the main deity of the temple. The other deities are Prāṇāmbikā, त्यागराज, Nīlotpalāmbikā and विनायक.
The Śanaiścara temple is just outside, the image being in a niche.
King Naḷa who was under the malefic influence of शनि, worshipped this शिव and got rid of all of his troubles. Hence he stayed here for some time and dug a tank which now bears his name as Naḷatīrtham. The deity itself got the name Nallar and Nallatra Īśar.
Later he worshipped शनि also and received his blessings. This शनि henceforward became very famous and started attracting a large number of devotees.
The image is black in colour with one hand showing abhayamudrā (assuring protection) which is rather rare. There is a golden crow which is his mount.
Five pūjas are performed everyday to this deity. Saturday is considered as a sacred day to worship him.
The festivals normally celebrated are:
Ādipūram; Ambu;ब्रह्मोत्सव and Rathotsava (April-May for 18 days)
Navarātrikolu, Śivarātri (February-March)
Vināyakacaturthī (September)

A very important festival is held for two days whenever the planet शनि leaves one राशि (zodiacal sign) and enters the next, which will last for 2 1/2 years. This is called Śanipeyārci. During this festival lakhs of devotees gather at this temple.

Tiruppāvai
(‘holy vow’)
------------------------------------------
This is a very famous poetical treatise in Tamil composed by आण्डाऌ (or Godādevī). (See ĀḶVĀRS for details.)
There are thirty pāśuras or verses. आण्डाऌ imagines that she is one of the गोपीस् performing the special कात्यायनी-vrata to get कृष्ण as their husband. In her imagination, Śrīvilliputtūr (her little town) becomes Nandagokula and the temple of Vaṭapatraśāyin (Viṣṇu) becomes नन्द’s palace. She goes about the streets of the town in the early morning, waking up her girl-friends, to go to the यमुना river for bath and worship!
This highly poetical treatise is centred round कृष्ण-भक्ति, love of कृष्ण as one’s lover and husband.
This work has been commented upon by innumerable scholars.
All the verses have been set to मुसिच् and are very popular. Singing them as also discourses on them during Dhanur-māsa or Mārgaśira (usually in December-January) has become a tradition among the Śrīvaiṣṇavas.

Tirumala-Tirupati
------------------------------------------
Whether religion is the opium of the masses or not, Lord Veṅkaṭeśvara of तिरुपति has certainly been casting a hypnotic (= devotional) spell on lakhs of devotees for centuries.
Tirumala is the range of seven hills forming a part of the Eastern Ghats. The main temple is on the seventh hill at a height of 840 metres (2800 feet) above the sea level. तिरुपति is the township at the foot of the hill.
The hill which is supposed to be a piece of the Meruparvata (See MERU.) has several names such as Śeṣācala, Vṛṣabhācala, Garuḍācala, Añjanādrī, Nārāyaṇādri, Siṁhācala and Veṅkaṭādri.
However, the original name was Veṅgaḍa, a Tamil word. In course of time it was Sanskritised to Veṅkaṭa. And, the god on this hill became वेङ्कटेश or Veṅkaṭeśvara or Veṅkaṭanātha.
Since the hill was also known as Śrīgiri, the lord of the hill became Śrīgirivāsa or श्रीनिवास also. बालाजी is another well-known name by which he is known.
The stone image of Lord Veṅka-ṭeśvara is believed to be svayaṁvyakta or self-manifested and not man-made. A great devotee of God, Raṅgadāsa by name, and Gopīnātha, another devotee, are said to have discovered this image which had been partially buried under the earth and redeemed it. Originally it might have been in the open and gradually by stages, the गर्भगृह (sanctum) and other parts of a regular temple might have been added, spread over some centuries.
तिरुपति.jpg" src="http://eoh.rkmathbangalore.org/public/images/thumbs/Tirumala-तिरुपति.jpg" alt="A View of Lord Veṅkaṭeśvara Temple">A View of Lord Veṅkaṭeśvara TempleIf the local legends have to be believed, a king Toṇḍamān (57 B. C.—A.
) by name seems to have built the first structure to protect the image. The antiquity of the image is further proved by the references to it in the ancient Tamil work Śilappadikāram (A.

th to the 8th centuries) in their pāśuras (verses) numbering 203.
As described in the epigraphical inscriptions, more than a thousand of which are available now, a few important stages in the evolution of the temple structure and rituals may now be noted:
Sāmavai, queen of the Pallava king, शक्ति-viṭaṅkaṭa, presented a silver image of the deity with all the ornaments (in A.

) to be kept in the main shrine for worship, after the same is performed for the chief deity.
Rāmānuja (A.

-1529) was significant. His bronze image, along with those of his two wives, is found in the मण्डप (hall) that bears his name.
The temple of Lord Veṅkaṭeśvara is situated on the last of the seven hills at a distance of 20 kms. (12 miles) by road from the town of तिरुपति at the foot of the hills. It is 126.5 metres (414 feet) long and 80 metres (263 feet) wide.
The विमान (tower above the sanctum) stands on a square base (each side being 8.3 metres or 27 feet) and has two tiers. It rises to a height of 11.3 metres or 37 feet. It is covered with gold plated copper sheets. It is called ‘Ānandanilaya’ (the abode of bliss).
Probably built in A.
, the golden cover of the विमान was renovated during A.

-58.
The primary path of circumambulation known as Vimānapradakṣiṇa, surrounds the main temple structure. It is 70.5 metres (235 feet) by 48 metres (160 feet).
The main temple structure comprises the following sections: ध्वजस्तम्भ (flag post); बलिपीठ (a stone platform for subsidiary offerings); a small गोपुर or tower over the entrance; मुखमण्डप (called tirumāmaṇimaṇḍapa, for accommodating the devotees before the final darśan of the deity); baṅgāru-vākili (golden door) with dvārapālakas (images of god’s gatekeepers) on either side; snapana-मण्डप (a small room where, perhaps the original metal images used to be bathed); śayāna-मण्डप (the place where the उत्सवमूर्ति is brought in the night for śayana or sleeping); the गर्भगृह (sanctum sanctorum).
The गर्भगृह is a square room (3.8 metres or 12.75 feet square) with thick walls (2.2 metres or 7 feet in thickness) covering three sides. The विमान is built on the outermost wall.
The dhruvabera—the main image—is fixed exactly in the centre of the sanctum. Its height is estimated to be between 2.4 to 2.7 metres (8 to 9 feet), since no one is allowed to actually measure it. Whether it is made of the black stone (śālagrāma śilā) or a kind of wood like redwooded fig tree (= raktacandana tree), it is difficult to say.
Since it does not conform to any of the rules laid in the works on Hindu इचोनोग्रफ्य् or the descriptions given in the dhyānaślokas (meditation verses) of the various aspects of विष्णु, the belief that it is svayaṁvyakta is strengthened.
On the chest, towards the right, is a symbol of लक्ष्मी, described as an icon seated on a lotus.
There are four hands. The two hands at the back hold the चक्र (discus) and शङ्ख (conch). The front right hand is showing the varada मुद्रा (boon giving pose). The left rests on the waist.
Lord VeṅkaṭeśvaraSome other aspects of the image like long hair, the peculiar conical crown, nāgavalaya (snake shaped ornament) as also certain ritual procedures like offering of बिल्व leaves and decorating with saree on Fridays has given rise to doubts regarding the deity it represents. Guesses galore have made it an image of विष्णु, शिव, देवी, सुब्रह्मण्य or हरिहर! As mentioned before, it is Rāmānuja who is said to have finally settled the disputes by declaring that it is that of विष्णु.
A special feature of the decorated image is the nāma or त्रिपुण्ड्र, the well-known caste mark of the श्रीवैष्णव sect. It is prepared out of paccakarpūra (a kind of camphor) and kastūri (musk), and covers the two eyes, the whole of the nose and extends on the forehead up to the crown. Applying this type of nāma is said to have begun in A.

.
There are other images in the sanctum as follows: Maṇavāḷapperumāḷ (silver image presented by the queen Sāmavai, also called भोग-श्रीनिवास); Ugra-श्रीनिवास with the images of Śrīdevī and भूदेवी; Maleyappa (a bigger image of Veṇkateśvara used for processional purposes); Koluvu-श्रीनिवास (used ceremonially like a king, everyday, before whom accounts of the day have to be given); कृष्ण; राम; सुदर्शन (discus-deity).
Inside the main temple campus, there are small shrines dedicated to वरदराज and नरसिṁह (two forms of विष्णु), राम, as also Rāmānuja.
It is interesting to note that in one of the old rooms, several copper plates containing the songs (etched on them) of अण्णमाचार्य (A.

-1503) on Lord Veṅkaṭeśvara were discovered. These songs are now being printed and widely used.
In this temple, it is the वैखानस आगम system of worship and rituals that is being followed for several centuries, as against the Pāñcarātra system which is much more common, especially in the Vaiṣṇava temples of South India. (See VAIKHĀNASA ĀGAMAS.)
Apart from the regular daily worship there are several other rites and rituals like tomālasevā (decorating with flower garlands), phūlaṅgisevā (similar to the previous one, but performed only on Thursdays) and tirumañjana (bathing the image, once a week, on Fridays only).
Among the various festivals of the temple the biggest and the most impressive is the ब्रह्मोत्सव, celebrated during the Navarātri festival (generally in September/October) for nine days. The रथोत्सव (temple-car festival) is held on the 8th day. On the last day, the उत्सवमूर्ति (processional deity) is bathed in the nearby temple-tank known as Svāmipuṣkariṇī (or Varāhatīrtha, because of the Varāha temple on its bank).
The temple is also famous for its prasāda, sacred offering in the form of laḍḍus (round shaped sweets) which are sold in millions.
This Veṅkaṭeśvara temple of Tirumala is not only the most popular but also the wealthiest in India.
Apart from a good motorable road (20 kms. or 12.5 miles) there are also well-laid steps (about 4000) by which earnest devotees can climb the hill from तिरुपति, up to the temple campus. It is 11 kms. (or 7 miles) in distance.
Other places of interest in Tirumala are—apart from the Svāmipuṣkariṇī tank and the Varāha temple—the Ākāśagaṅgā falls, Pāpanāśaṁ-tīrtha, Kumāradhārā and a few more sources of holy waters.
At the foot of the hills is तिरुपति, the main city. The temples of Govindarāja, Kodaṇḍarāma and Kapileśvara (Śiva) are situated here.
The Govindarājā temple contains the older shrine of Pārthasārathi (Kṛṣṇa) dating back to the 9th century A. D. as also that of Govindarāja established by Rāmānuja in A.

. The deity here is a शयानमूर्ति (in the lying posture) as in the श्रीरङ्गम् temple. It has an impressive gopuram (tower) of seven storeys.
About 2 kms. (1.2 miles) away from the above temple, is the Kodanḍarāma temple built in A.

.
Another important temple included in the तिरुपति पिल्ग्रिमगे is the पद्मावती temple at Tiruccānūr, 5 kms. (3 miles) away from the तिरुपति town.
Padmāvatī—also called Alarmelmaṅgai—is the consort of Lord Veṅka-ṭeśvara. Her icon is shown as seated in the पद्मासन style and holding a lotus in each of the upper two hands. The lower hands are in the abhaya and varada mudrās, giving protection as also granting boons.
Once in a year, there is a big festival celebrating the मर्रिअगे of पद्मावती with Veṅkaṭeśvara. Her processional image is taken on an elephant to the Tirumala temple, where he ‘comes out’ to meet her! The ब्रह्मोत्सव of this temple is on the ‘birthday’ of पद्मावती, generally in November/December.
The ‘Tirumala-तिरुपति-Devasthānams’ (T.T.D. for short) is a huge organisation entrusted with the management of the main temple, allied temples and other institutions. The fabulous income of the temples is being utilised for the welfare of the pilgrims by providing many facilities like rest-houses, free-ड़ोओद् and prasāda (consecrated ड़ोओद्) as also transportation. It is also running a university with several academic institutions affiliated to it, including an Oriental research institute.
